paperTitle: O-Level English 1184 Paper 2 Section B — The Durian
note: AI-authored original narrative for O-Level §B style practice; not from a past examination paper. 出处说明仅作内部记录，不得写进 passage 正文（学生可见）。 2026-08-11 2.0 改造：原 Q6-Q8 三道 2 分 prose 拆成六道 1 分单选（得分点不变，只把「写出来」换成「选出来」）；原 Q9-Q10 保留为 prose并加结构脚手架，作为卷内对照组；Q1-Q5 加答案长度提示。分值仍为 15。

sections.instruction: Read the narrative text below and answer the questions that follow. Section B, Part 1 [15 marks]. Answer in your own words as far as possible.
sections.passage:
Paragraph 1
My father brought home a durian on the last Friday of every month. He carried it in a red plastic bag held out from his body at arm's length, as though it were something that might change its mind. We would hear the lift doors, then his key, then the bag going down on the kitchen floor, and the whole flat would fill with that smell within about four seconds.

Paragraph 2
He opened it himself, always. He put down two sheets of newspaper, sat on the low plastic stool, wedged the point of the knife into the seam at the bottom and worked it until the shell gave with a sound like a small door. Inside, the flesh sat in its compartments, pale gold, and he would hold the first one up and look at it for a moment before passing it to my grandmother, who ate it very slowly with her eyes shut.

Paragraph 3
Then my mother. Then my sister. Then me. There were usually five or six pieces in a good one, and my father took the last, or if there were only five, he took none, and said he had eaten too much at lunch. He said this so regularly that for years I simply believed it, the way you believe that the lift is slow or that Fridays come after Thursdays.

Paragraph 4
I was fourteen when I went with him. It was raining and he wanted help with the umbrella. The stall was under a shophouse five stops away on the bus, and I watched him do a thing I had never seen him do: he stood at the front of the pile for a long time, picking up one fruit and then another, shaking each one beside his ear, tapping the shell with a knuckle, putting it down. The seller waited. My father moved along the whole row and came back to one he had already put down twice.

Paragraph 5
Then he asked the price. Then he asked it again about a smaller one at the back. He bought the smaller one. On the bus he held it on his lap and said nothing much, and I looked at the rain on the window and did the arithmetic I had never once thought to do: what he earned, what the fruit cost, what a month of Fridays came to.

Paragraph 6
That evening he opened it on the newspaper as usual. There were five pieces. My grandmother took the first with her eyes shut, and my mother, and my sister, and I took mine and did not eat it. I put it on the edge of the newspaper nearest him and said I was full. He looked at me for slightly too long. Then he said, 'Don't waste,' and ate it, and nothing else was said about it, and nothing else has ever been said about it since.

Paragraph 7
He still buys one on the last Friday of the month. He is slower on the stool now and he lets my sister's husband do the opening, though he still chooses the fruit himself, and still shakes it beside his ear, and still comes back to one he has put down twice.

Paragraph 8
People write a great deal about how much a father says and how little he explains. Mine never explained anything. He simply arranged, month after month, for there to be a thing in the house that everybody wanted and that he would not have — and he arranged it so quietly, and for so long, that his own children took nearly fifteen years to notice they were being given something.

(Glossary: shophouse: a traditional two- or three-storey building with a shop below and living space above; stool: a low plastic seat commonly used in Singapore kitchens.)

questions.stem: Q1. From Paragraph 1, how often did the narrator's father bring home a durian? （一句话即可） [1]
questions.answer: on the last Friday of every month / once a month

questions.stem: Q2. From Paragraph 3, what reason did the father give for not eating any durian? （一句话即可） [1]
questions.answer: that he had eaten too much at lunch

questions.stem: Q3. What does the phrase 'held out from his body at arm's length' (Paragraph 1) suggest about the durian? （写出它暗示了什么，一句话） [1]
questions.answer: that its smell was so strong and pungent that he kept it as far from himself as he could while still carrying it

questions.stem: Q4. What does the writer suggest by describing the shell as giving 'with a sound like a small door' (Paragraph 2)? （写出它暗示了什么，一句话） [1]
questions.answer: that it opened with a single sharp crack, and that opening it felt like being let into something / the start of an occasion

questions.stem: Q5. What does the word 'arithmetic' in 'did the arithmetic I had never once thought to do' (Paragraph 5) suggest about the narrator? （写出它暗示了什么，一句话） [1]
questions.answer: that he was working out the cost for the first time and realising, coldly and precisely, what the monthly durian meant against his father's wages

options.text: He had understood the sacrifice and wanted his father to eat some for once.

Q11. Why did he say he was "full" instead of explaining himself? [1]

options.text: He was afraid his father would be angry.
He used the same kind of excuse his father always used, so nothing had to be said aloud.
He could not think of the English words.
His grandmother had told him to stay quiet.

Q12. What is the effect of the father's response, 'Don't waste,' and of the fact that 'nothing else has ever been said about it since'? (Paragraph 6) [2]

作答提示：分两点写，每点一句话即可。① …… ② ……
questions.answer: the blunt two-word reply refuses the emotional moment and keeps the exchange practical, which is exactly how this family communicates; the years of silence that follow show that both understood perfectly and that the understanding did not need words — the restraint conveys far more warmth than a spoken thank-you would

questions.stem:
Q13. What is the effect of the final clause, 'took nearly fifteen years to notice they were being given something'? (Paragraph 8) [2]

作答提示：分两点写，每点一句话即可。① …… ② ……
questions.answer: the long stretch of time measures the father's steadiness against the children's obliviousness, so the sacrifice is made to seem larger for having gone unremarked; the plain word 'something', left deliberately unnamed, suggests the gift was never really the fruit at all
